patch.objective: Recognize opioid-induced oversedation with a sedation scale before respiratory depression, and respond
secondaryObjectives: Recognize patient, drug, environment and equipment risk factors for harm

sources.cite: MSNCB, 2023 CMSRN Exam Blueprint: Patient/Care Management (32%)
sources.note: Relayed from the CMSRN course seed (backend/supabase/seed/tracks/cmsrn.ts), which read the blueprint 2026-11-14, not re-read for this band. Patient/Care Management covers the nursing process, safety, medication and pre- and post-procedure care. Scope only.
The objective and secondary objectives are the course's own titles.

sources.cite: Pasero Opioid-Induced Sedation Scale (POSS) with interventions, as reproduced by RNAO (Registered Nurses' Association of Ontario) best practice guideline pages
sources.note: Relayed from the ADN-RN case pca-oversedation-naloxone, not re-read for this band; its note: Read 2026-11-11 (the RNAO reproduction, not Pasero's original 1994 publication). S and 1-2 acceptable; 3 (frequently drowsy, arousable, drifts off to sleep during conversation) unacceptable: monitor closely until stable below 3, decrease the opioid dose 25-50% or notify the prescriber; 4 (somnolent, minimal or no response to verbal or physical stimulation) unacceptable: stop the opioid, consider naloxone, notify the prescriber, monitor closely.

sources.cite: Pfizer. Naloxone Hydrochloride Injection, prescribing information (dosage, clinical pharmacology, warnings, precautions)
sources.note: Relayed from the ADN-RN case pca-oversedation-naloxone, not re-read for this band; its note: Read 2026-11-11 (primary web pages). Postoperative opioid depression: 0.1 to 0.2 mg IV at two to three minute intervals to the desired degree of reversal, titrated to response; larger than necessary doses can reverse analgesia and raise blood pressure; abrupt postoperative reversal may cause nausea, vomiting, sweating, tremulousness, tachycardia, and has been followed by ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation, pulmonary edema and cardiac arrest. IV onset generally within two minutes; serum half-life in adults 30 to 81 min (mean 64); the duration of some opioids may exceed naloxone's, so keep the patient under continued surveillance and repeat doses as needed.

sources.cite: Pfizer. Hydromorphone Hydrochloride Injection, prescribing information (clinical pharmacology)
sources.note: Relayed from the ADN-RN case pca-oversedation-naloxone, not re-read for this band; its note: Read 2026-11-11 (primary web page). Terminal elimination half-life after an IV dose about 2.3 hours.

sources.cite: Jungquist CR, et al. American Society for Pain Management Nursing guidelines on monitoring for opioid-induced advancing sedation and respiratory depression: revisions. Pain Manag Nurs 2020;21(1):7-25. doi:10.1016/j.pmn.2019.06.007
sources.note: Relayed from the ADN-RN case pca-oversedation-naloxone, not re-read for this band; its note: Read only through a summary (University at Buffalo School of Nursing news item, 2020-01-24, read 2026-11-11); the publisher page did not load. The summary says the revisions update the 2011 guidelines for hospitalized adults on opioids, add more specific recommendations for electronic monitoring and introduce three categories of risk factors. No number in this case is taken from it.
